Hey [~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a] 

CS agents should not use templated responses unless there’s some specific information that we must include to avoid legal repercussions. As this template is simply a message to inform the rider that we’re investigating, CS agents can write a message on their own. So, we have replaced the template below with the instruction, “Advise the customer that we've escalated the issue to our specialists.”

{quote}_Hey [Name],_

_Thank you for bringing this to our attention. We have escalated this issue to our specialist team who are currently investigating this issue. We ask for your patience while our specialist team works to take appropriate action to address your concerns._

_If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this message._

_Sincerely,_

_Bolt_{quote}

However, the template that explains to the driver that we’re suspending the account will be included in the process to ensure that we communicate the necessary information to the driver. I have made some small amendments, so the version we will publish is:

{quote}After a thorough investigation, we regrettably discovered that your account on our platform has been engaging in suspicious and unusual activities that indicate attempted phishing and/or other scams.

According to our terms of service, which you agreed to upon registration, any fraudulent and/or suspicious activity, such as phishing, is strictly prohibited on our platform. Violation of these terms results in immediate termination of the user account.

Due to the urgent suspicion that you, or someone with access to your account, have been involved in phishing activities, we are compelled to suspend your user account with immediate effect and terminate the contract without notice.  

This measure serves to protect our users and the integrity of our platform. 

If you have any questions or objections regarding this decision, you can contact our Customer Service team. We will review each case separately and carefully.{quote}

Let us know if there are any issues with this approach 🙏

{code:sql}SELECT
date(date_trunc('week',x.created)) AS week,
APPROX_DISTINCT(x.id,0.0041) AS count_orders,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(x.user_price_eur) AS double),2) AS user_price_sum_eur,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.is_initial_failed_payment OR x.initial_failed_eur > 0 THEN x.id END,0.0041) AS count_ifp,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.is_initial_failed_payment OR x.initial_failed_eur > 0 THEN x.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(x.id,0.0041) AS double),3),0) AS ratio_ifp,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.is_final_failed_payment OR x.uncovered_eur > 0 THEN x.id END,0.0041) AS count_fp,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.is_final_failed_payment OR x.uncovered_eur > 0 THEN x.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(x.id,0.0041) AS double),3),0) AS ratio_fp,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_initial_failed_payment OR x.initial_failed_eur > 0 THEN x.initial_failed_eur END) AS double),2),0) AS ifp_sum_eur,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_initial_failed_payment OR x.initial_failed_eur > 0 THEN x.initial_failed_eur END) AS double),2),0)*1.000/SUM(x.user_price_eur) AS double),3),0) AS ifp_sum_ratio,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_final_failed_payment OR x.uncovered_eur > 0 THEN x.uncovered_eur END) AS double),2),0) AS fp_sum_eur,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_final_failed_payment OR x.uncovered_eur > 0 THEN x.uncovered_eur END) AS double),2),0)*1.000/SUM(x.user_price_eur) AS double),3),0) AS fp_sum_ratio,
ROUND(CAST((1 - SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_final_failed_payment OR x.uncovered_eur > 0 THEN x.uncovered_eur END)/SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_initial_failed_payment OR x.initial_failed_eur > 0 THEN x.initial_failed_eur END)) AS double),3) AS recovery_rate
FROM (
WITH gateway AS (
SELECT DISTINCT 
a.order_id,
a.gateway
FROM ng_commerce.payments_etl a
WHERE a.created_date >= date '2024-07-01'
),
count_destinations AS (
SELECT b.city_id,
b.order_id,
COUNT(*)-1 as count_of_destinations_changes
FROM ng_public.company_order_destination b
LEFT JOIN ng_public.admin_system_city sc ON b.city_id = sc.id
WHERE b.created_date >= date '2024-07-01'
AND sc.country_code = 'ng'																										 
GROUP BY 1,2	
)
SELECT DISTINCT 
etl.id,
etl.created,
etl.payment_method_type,
etl.uncovered_amount*1.00/etl.eur_currency_rate AS uncovered_eur,
etl.initial_failed_payment_amount*1.00/etl.eur_currency_rate AS initial_failed_eur,
etl.is_initial_failed_payment,
etl.is_final_failed_payment,
etl.user_price_eur
FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders AS etl 
JOIN gateway g ON g.order_id = etl.booking_id
LEFT JOIN count_destinations cd ON etl.order_id = cd.order_id AND etl.city_id = cd.city_id  
WHERE etl.created_date >= date '2024-07-01'
AND etl.country_code = 'ng'	 
AND etl.order_type = 'rides'
AND etl.order_state = 'finished' 	
AND etl.payment_method_group IN ('in-app','bolt_credit')																								
AND etl.payment_method_type <> 'business'						
AND g.gateway = 'paystack'
AND cd.count_of_destinations_changes > 0
) AS x
GROUP BY 1 
ORDER BY 1 DESC{code}

Hello Edgaras,

Thank you for your feedback, I’ll address the issues you flagged one by one: 

*- Answer option states “shifts blame on the provider” rather than “rider”.* → Fixed

*- Training material states that the formal ways of signing off should be used when communicating with authorities, yet the example shows the formal sign-off being used in communicaion with regular user;* → I replaced the “Regards” with “Have a nice day,” so the sign-off is less formal, but if we think about formal sign-offs they are usually “Yours faithfully”, and “Yours sincerely”. “Regards” is less formal than these two and more neutral. 

*- Speculation in the example message (Driver called you probably to find out)* → I see your point, I deleted the “probably to find out where he could pick you up” part. 🙂 

-*Use of negative language in example (it didn't work out)* → In this case “it didn’t work out” is not considered negative language. Negative language is not defined only by the use of “no”, but by the meaning or the intention of the communication, here are some examples: 
1. Negative language is non-communication : “I wouldn’t do it that way.”, “There is nothing I can do”
2. Negative language is confusing: “I don’t disagree”, “I can’t speak for them,”
3. Negative language is destructive: “I don’t believe you,” “I don’t think it happened like that”
4. Negative language is heavy: “No one believes you,” “That’s a lie,”

*Reply from quality*: Wouldn’t consider this negative language, there’s a difference between acknowledging a ”negative” situation and inappropriate use of negative language. It would be a different story if the agent then said “If you keep ordering Bolt to places the driver can’t pick you up, they’ll keep canceling it”. 

- *Training material notes to use a comma ahter the greeting, before the user's name - it is absent here.* → Greeting punctuation rules can differ by country from what I know. People also use: *_Hello, name,_* or *_Hello, name!_*, but *_Hello name,_* is also fine ([here is an article form the British Council.|https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/business-english/english-emails/unit-4-starting-finishing-emails])

- *Written support course, Education and Warning section: the "Continue" button for most examples does not work.* → I tested them now and there was only one that wasn’t working, and it’s fixed now. In most cases the “Continue” button leads you to a second case.

*Phone support course contains a glitch in audio examples, where upon pausing an example and then resuming, will cause multiple examples to start playing simultaneously.* -> this is indeed a technical issue, I temporarily removed the play/pause button until we get it fixed.  

*The section on out bound calls fails to elaborate on what should be done if the user is unwilling or unable to speak. This is especiall important if the call is being made due to urgent matters.* → There are 2 more examples for greeting:

- I am reaching out to you about the payment issue you reported yesterday. *_Do you have a few spare minutes to talk?_* and 

- Hi, Sam! It’s Mary from Bolt Support. I am reaching out about a phone that one of your passengers lost today. *_Is it okay for you to talk right now?_* 

*The Food Delivery example uses filler word during phone conversation (Hmmmm).* → there is not problem doing this, it’s natural to happen.

*Replay from quality:* Agreed with training, wouldn’t consider it a filler word, it actually almost adds onto the acknowledgment in the beginning, kind of a silent agreement with the “hm”.

Bad payment rides refer to orders where an in-app payment results in a failed payment, chargeback, or other payment issues (e.g., notifications from issuing banks about problematic payments) combined with some other suspicious indicators such as close pick up distance or unusually expensive price. It does not deduct any money from driver balance however if a driver accumulates a significant number of such “bad payments,” it indicates that the driver is likely involved in fraud and therefore gets blocked by the system which was not the case for this driver.

Of course, there can be false-positive cases for any fraud pattern, and these orders appear to be one of those cases. If you notice a significant number of false positives in your market, please create a business case (preferably with monetary impact), and we will review the thresholds for your market.

A few other general questions / points to note on this ticket, just to ensure that relevant teams have visibility of the process and to ensure that we are taking a streamlined approach in response to these cases:

* To the extent possible, we should ensure that we are developing *global* processes to deal with compromised accounts, which contain market-specific sections. Otherwise, creating divergent practices in different markets will result in inconsistencies and increase escalation risk. Please ensure that both [~accountid:5e592fc129e6d00c9707e3b5] and the CS Knowledge Team are keep in the loop in this regard, particularly where similar work on this may have already been done in other markets (e.g., Kenya and Malta).
* We should ensure that we have a process in place that has been approved by InfoSec to determine the *likelihood that an account has actually been compromised*. In the UK case, we have been referring to factors such as whether a user has specifically complained about compromise, whether any new devices have been added which we recognise as being added to other similar accounts, whether the account name has been changed to one we recognise etc., but if we agreeing on a global process then we should make sure that this forms a part of it.
* Where we are reasonably certain that an account has been compromised, the privacy team should be looped in (by raising a personal data incident ticket [here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/47]), as this may constitute a *personal data breach*, which we will need to review and assess. If a global process is being agreed, then notifying the privacy team in cases of compromises accounts should feature as part of the process.
* Do we know whether a process is also being developed for *rider* accounts? What is being done in cases of riders whose accounts are compromised in this way?
* Finally - a potential suggestion - is there any scope for implementing a new part of the registration process whereby the user enters a ‘backup email address’, which cannot subsequently be accessed / edited on the account? When account takeover has happened, we could then use the backup email address for the purpose of assisting the genuine account owner with regaining access.

Hello [~accountid:712020:7f0b3550-60c0-44c1-ab18-391c6e0b8688] 

back in July 2023 the authority “_Défenseur des droits_” reached out to Bolt France regarding an alleged cas of discrimination of a passenger wearing a FFP2 mask that has been dropped off by the driver before final destination (see below an exhaustive description of the facts). The Authority asked Bolt to provide information  about the sanctions applied by Bolt against the driver and our reporting procedures in the event of discriminatory behaviour perpetrated by a driver. 

This case raised awareness on a risk lying on the platform because of discriminatory acts perpetrated by drivers. Indeed, Bolt could potentially be found liable of discrimination, in civil and criminal procedures, in claims raised against drivers and Bolt. In this instance, the _Defenseur des droits_ has confirmed that as a platform Bolt could be held liable for the drivers’ actions. 



*The facts:* 

* A customer wearing a mask was asked by the driver upon entering the vehicle if he was suffering from Covid 19. The customer explained that he had cancer. Shortly afterwards (2 minutes after the customer was charged according to the Customer Service), he saw his ride stopped by the driver who invoked a technical issue.
* The customer contacted Customer Service, who offered him a 5 euros voucher. It was told to the customer that the behaviour of the driver would be investigated, and that proper measures would be taken against them. 
* The customer referred the case to the _Defenseur des droits_. 
* The Authority contacted Bolt and communications were exchanged. 

* Regarding Bolt internal process, the driver was contacted by Bolt, who reminded them to remain courteous with the customers.



*Findings:* 

The Authority, without condemning Bolt, shared an opinion that Bolt could be sentenced for discriminatory acts coming from the drivers, during potential civil and criminal proceedings. 

The Authority made a reminder of the current law: to discriminate against someone by refusing a service to them can lead to up to 3 years of imprisonment as well as a fine of up to 45.000 euros (articles 225-1 and 225-2 of the French _Code penal_). And, in France when there is an assumption of discrimination, this will be to the defendant to prove the case (article 4 of the law 2008-496 of the 27 May 2008).

The Authority mentioned that in case of a lawsuit, there is a high probability that Bolt could be considered as the employer of the driver, and declared guilty of discrimination. 



+Current procedure in case of a discriminatory claim+: 



!https://lh7-qw.googleusercontent.com/docsz/AD_4nXdL_wQL-sZqoeCrGzVOughQ80AeqOEcXoWx6LUW07XB9BPrRtoEbz55JsF7pvHPet7Wa9hC1JjeoLdiH7M0WJUF9Q2qsFc574e-dfyqmRxnoYWzm7GY27rdEGFVGiSVNB0OjCEAddaYr7tYa4n6gtL6jJfL?key=5Q_CiUE3PlqB8NVVD8SBUw|width=1456,height=522!

*Conclusion and general comment:* 

This is escalated to you [~accountid:712020:7f0b3550-60c0-44c1-ab18-391c6e0b8688] on a FYI basis. However, should similar events occur and should the frequency increase, we should work alongside to raise awareness among the drivers about discriminatory behaviours that would trigger some liability for the platform. 



Thanks,

Michela

h3. They not only solve the problem in ticket but also improve experience (and lineage!)

* *_Running Ingestion without sources_* 
* *_Generating manifests for every dbt project and ingesting them one by one_*

h3. Running Ingestion without sources

Good temporary (even for a long time) solution.

h4. *_Pros_*

* Fixes overwrites of dbt models with sources (lost column descriptions as stated in the ticket, broken lineage with cycles and missing nodes)

h4. *_Cons_*

* We won’t have sources as a SubType like we do now, might look a little incomplete

    # Options
    target_platform: glue
    entities_enabled:
      sources: "NO"

transformers:
    ...{noformat}

I advise we push to include the below two points:

According to Section 30 of the German Road Traffic Act (StVO), so-called "Spaßfahrten", i.e. driving back and forth unnecessarily, are prohibited. 

An e-scooter is considered a motor vehicle within the meaning of the StVO, which is why this ban also applies to e-scooters in principle, but it should not be forbidden to use the word "fun rides" in advertising, although we should be extremely careful that our advertising does not directly or indirectly encourage such rides. 

Even if violations are merely misdemeanors (Ordnungswidrigkeiten) and therefore would not constitute an incitement to commit a crime and therefore legal reprisals are unlikely to be feared, we must ensure that we neither trivialize the issue nor give the impression that such rides are legally and practically unproblematic.

In this particular case, I consider the risk of legal reprisals to be rather low. Bolt explicitly shows no positive or approving attitude towards such rides in its advertising by crossing out the word "fun rides". However, it would be worth considering clearly pointing out in the communication that fun rides are considered an offense. * If the rider does not refer to either: (a) personal data processing / privacy law; or (b) individual / average rider ratings in their request, we should just be referring the rider to general informative materials on how Rider Ratings are calculated (e.g. [https://bolt.eu/en/rider-rating/|https://bolt.eu/en/rider-rating/]).
* If the rider refers to personal data / privacy law in a request concerning how Rider Ratings work, we should effectively just refer them to the relevant sections of Bolt’s privacy notice.
* If the rider requests individual rider ratings, we should not be providing this data if it can be used to identify specific drivers (e.g., if a rider requests a rating for one specific trip, we definitely should not provide it). We _could_ take the approach that if the rider has taken a lot of trips, then we just provide a list of the individual ratings without matching them to dates and times - however, this approach is not without risk. I think this is the key point that we should discuss with the wider team.

Instead, the rider should be referred to *general informative materials* on rider ratings. It should then be left to the rider to request more specific information, if they want it.

hey [~accountid:5e592fc129e6d00c9707e3b5],

Getting back to you with further questions and concerns:

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Informing users and Blocking them*
{panel}

* Concern here is that *we should provide information to users why they are blocked*. In this case, blocking the user and providing details about the ride or situation can *impede on the investigation of the police.*
* In most of the laws of EU countries, *Bolt is not entitled to disclose to users any information about the police contacting Bolt or the situation.* It means that we would need to:
** Analyse whether Bolt is entitled to disclose any information to user and whether such a blocking would be a violation of such provisions
** In the best scenario, Bolt would need to ask for the police consent to actively proceed with the internal investigation and blocking, ensuring it’s not an impediment for them
* *Blocking users due to the police report can be unjustifiable as this is still an allegation.* Of course, currently, we block users in case one of the users reports the incident to us, but it’s still not ideal scenario to deny the services based on allegations.
** How would we unblock users? 
** As I understood, you would communicate with both parties to understand the situation and then decide whether to block the user permanently or unblock. However, the decision of the police/court could be different, eg the user is recognised innocent or guilty while Bolt’s investigation is the opposite. What would Bolt do in such cases?

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Stats on cases that happened via Bolt platform*
{panel}

* *You mentioned that we need to conduct investigations only on police reports alleging the case happened via Bolt platform.* 
** Can you advise how many of such cases we have? In most of the cases, users just use Bolt services and this is how they can be related to the crime, but we are not aware of a lot of cases when someone used Bolt for criminal actions.
** What do you mean by cases happened via Bolt (like violating our T&Cs)? In most of the cases, every situation can be recognised as happened via Bolt if there were any link to Bolt.
** Would you consider a case as committed using Bolt platform if the user is just a rider /driver on a platform, but hasn’t used Bolt for this?

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Competitors and Purpose*
{panel}

* Have you investigated whether any of our competitors do the same with their users? 
* What is the specific purpose of doing such a blocking and investigation from the police report? can it help with eliminating a lot of criminal cases on a platform (based on any approximate statistics)?

Summary, while we  understand the process would be the same as for our current blocking process and instead of users submitting their complaint to us, it would be a police; however, there are still above concerns that cannot green light this project. 



*The main concern is the police investigation impediment and potential violation of EU laws when stepping in any investigation in parallel.*

Hey [~accountid:5e3d437d9749d00c924cb0f5], when a third party (such as a friend or family member, attorney, or anyone else) informs us of a driver's death and requests account deletion, we should proceed as follows:

* Ask the requestor to provide a proof of death - a valid death certificate or other official documentation as proof of the driver's death. This will help us verify whether the driver in question is really deceased, and, therefore, whether privacy laws apply.
* We need to check whether the information provided by the requestor matches the driver’s data that we have to make sure we delete the correct account.
* Upon receiving the information, analysing the provided data and verifying the proof of death, delete the driver's account. 

❗ If the data provided in the request does not match the driver’s data, or if we do not receive proof of death, we shall not delete the account.

One important thing - this only applies to drivers, and not passengers.

+*Summary*+

* I agree with the position that hard opt-in is required in Poland for any kind of direct marketing/outbound sales activities. 
* As of 10 November 2024 new act  that repeals the whole Telecommunications Act and Article 10 of the PSEM will be in force, therefore there will be only one regulation that concerns consents for marketing.
* I believe that DLP’s opinion results from the fact that (as of today) there are 2 acts that relate to consents for direct marketing which create lots of confusion and various understanding of both acts and relationship between them. 
* In my opinion, DLP’s position is a minority one, so taking into consideration that Polish authorities are very strict in this area, I would not recommend it (Polish authorities even present a position that contacting the end-user to obtain his/her consent should be considered as a direct marketing activity which generally means that you are not allowed to offer any products of services if you have not obtained prior consent in any other way). On the other hand, Polish courts usually present slightly less strict position and - in this specific case (judgment of the Warsaw-Praga Regional Court of 4 January 2019, IV Ca 1873/16) - even allowed to contact a consumer to obtain his/her consent for direct marketing.
* *Taking into consideration that the Article 398 of the New Act (defined below) is based on the Article 172 of the Telecommunications Act (which is now considered as more “strict” act than the PSEM) which applies to both physical persons and legal entities, I consider contacting other people with Bolt’s offer as risky, unless point 2 above is met or Bolt receives prior consent for marketing contacts.*

+*New act to be in force as of 10 November 2024*+

On 9 August 2024 the Polish president signed an Electronic Communication Act (the *“New Act*”) that *repeals the whole Telecommunications Act and Article 10 of the PSEM* (the PSEM Act will remain in force in most part). The New Act *enters in force on 10 November 2024* (some provisions enter later but they do not concern the discussed issue).  *As a result, there will be one act that governs the issue of consent to direct marketing.*

Article 398 of the New Act is generally very similar to the current Article 172 of the Telecommunications Act:

# _It is prohibited to use:_
# _automatic calling systems,_
# _telecommunications terminal equipment, in particular in the use of interpersonal communication services_

_for the purpose of sending commercial information within the meaning of the provisions of the Act of July 18, 2002 on the provision of services by electronic means (Journal of Laws of 2020, item 344 and of 2024, item 1222), including direct marketing, to a subscriber or end-user, unless he/she has previously given his/her consent._

# *_The consent referred to in paragraph 1 may be given by the subscriber or end-user by providing an electronic address identifying him or her within the meaning of the Act of July 18, 2002 on the provision of electronic services, for the purpose of sending commercial information to the electronic address provided by the subscriber or end-user._*
# _The use of the means referred to in paragraph 1 to send commercial information, including direct marketing, shall not be at the expense of the end user or subscriber._
# _The activity referred to in paragraph 1 shall constitute an act of unfair competition within the meaning of the provisions of the Act on Combating Unfair Competition of April 16, 1993 (Journal of Laws of 2022, item 1233)_

Thanks [~accountid:712020:b2a2738f-c1f1-447c-9b72-29851b5fed3e] - it looks like the first of your two questions should no longer apply. 

Regarding your second question, my thoughts are as follows. In short, *the main consideration here is whether an agreement is in place*, as opposed to whether that agreement mentions the relevant processing activities:

* The [EDPB guidance|https://www.edpb.europa.eu/sites/default/files/files/file1/edpb_guidelines-art_6-1-b-adopted_after_public_consultation_en.pdf] makes it clear that there must exist “_a valid contract with the data subject_” in order for the controller to rely on 6.1(b). As such, if there is no T&C, we need to make sure that some other form of binding agreement is in place.
* Re whether the conditions communicated to the drivers (without T&C) would still constitute a binding agreement if they decide to participate - this is a question of Lithuanian contract law. Although we could probably argue this, I personally would be more comfortable if there was something more explicit in the form (if no T&Cs apply) noting that the driver is ‘agreeing’ to participate - in any case, {color:#4c9aff}*I assume we should double-check this with the local legal team*{color}, for completeness? Otherwise I would be making assumptions about local contract law which may diverge from the UK position.
* Although the guidance states that “_processing may be objectively necessary even if not specifically mentioned in the contract_”, this extract is still housed in a more general paragraph that talks about the importance of the controller fulfilling its transparency obligations, and so if we do not include the information discussed below then _technically_ there is some non-compliance risk. Ultimately, however, given that the only data that it seems we are now collecting is name and email address, and the purpose of collection is clear (i.e., determining who will be invited to the event), {color:#36b37e}*we could take a risk-based approach and argue that it is obvious that the data processing happening here is objectively necessary to perform the agreement*{color} (and so does not need to be specifically mentioned) - what do you think?

Dear Вадим Ціхомський

 

*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 

 

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *25 July 2024.*

 

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 

 

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software.Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail,  we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

 

We will share copies of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

* *All trip history*

 

For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at [https://bolt.eu/en/legal/|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/] , which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

 

*Your rights* 

 

In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.

 

 

Yours sincerely,



Bolt

My experience - generally, it is possible, and common practice for campaigns such s competitions, sweepstakes, etc. However, it can be challenging due to GDPR principles such as transparency - basic privacy information must be provided, i.e. - adding a short privacy disclaimer and linking a privacy notice. Similar challenges arise when the contract is oral.

At Bolt, I always try to push for T&Cs, as we have a basic Campaign Template which is easily tailored + allows to avoid legal ambiguity as well (issues of liability, etc). This indeed cures legal and privacy risks.

The law seems to only regulate the production of hemp products, the supply of hemp products to the market, and the import of hemp products - Bolt would not be doing any of these (_supply of fiber hemp products and products to the market is defined as: holding fiber hemp products and products for sale, including offering for sale or any other means of transfer thereof, free of charge or for money, and the actual sale, distribution and other forms of transfer thereof_).

Dear Raúl Lopes

 

*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 

 

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *25 July 2024.*

 

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 

 

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software.Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail,  we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

 

We will share copies of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

* *Trip history from May to June*

 

For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at [Terms and Conditions|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/] , which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

 

*Your rights* 

 

In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.

 

 

Yours sincerely,



Bolt

Presto query for finding affected delivery campaigns

{code:sql}select mb.order_id, ubc.*
from ng_delivery.delivery_basket_master_basket mb,
     ng_delivery.delivery_basket_user_basket ub,
     ng_delivery.delivery_basket_campaign ubc
where mb.id = ub.master_basket_id
  and ubc.user_basket_id = ub.id
  and ubc.state = 'active'
  and ubc.target = 'delivery_price'
  and not exists (select 1 from ng_delivery.delivery_invoicing_record r where mb.order_id = r.order_id and r.type = 'deliveryCampaign')
  and exists (select 1 from ng_delivery.delivery_invoicing_record r where mb.order_id = r.order_id and r.type = 'delivery')
  and mb.state = 'closed'
order by mb.created desc;{code}

Presto query for V1 food campaigns.

{code:sql}select mb.order_id, ubc.*
from ng_delivery.delivery_basket_master_basket mb,
     ng_delivery.delivery_basket_user_basket ub,
     ng_delivery.delivery_basket_campaign ubc
where mb.id = ub.master_basket_id
  and ubc.user_basket_id = ub.id
  and ubc.state = 'active'
  and ubc.target in ('item_price', 'total_price')
  and ubc.cost_share_version = 'V1'
  and not exists (select 1 from ng_delivery.delivery_invoicing_record r where mb.order_id = r.order_id and r.type = 'foodCampaign')
  and exists (select 1 from ng_delivery.delivery_invoicing_record r where mb.order_id = r.order_id and r.type = 'food')
  and mb.state = 'closed'
order by mb.created desc;{code}

* the components indeed changed because of the dynamic start rate (a feature we are currently testing) that according to the ETA of the driver, the start rate and consequently the rate per km and min adjust.

* in this case, so we don’t get into these topics with the regulator and the driver, we can claim that our price can be calculated via 2 ways: sum of components or fixed price pre-approved by all the parties involved (as stated in our T&Cs). Therefore, in this case, we went for the second option and the price that showed on the driver app screen and that was accepted by him, matches the amount paid to the driver. Therefore, no adjustment needs to be made.

Flag “Partner pays commission using invoice”, internally called “partner_dual_account”.
It has to be switched midnight - for Commission Records assigned to 2024-08, the option should be disabled, but for Commission Records assigned to 2024-09-01, it should be enabled.

Hi [~accountid:712020:d63a9c49-7399-46e3-8b6f-3b8ca34dfafd] and [~accountid:712020:0b1ccfcb-3809-460a-88ab-c96985ba329a],
Thank you for the support on this. 

To elaborate more on this change of vendor. 

+*AppMan’s process:*+

Previously we have used AppMan as a vendor for the checks but their KYC (Know Your Customer) process requires an additional layer of consent from the drivers. Simply put, the drivers will go through two consents - one with Bolt and one with AppMan. This has resulted in high drop-off rates from the drivers to execute the checks.

+*iBoost’s process:*+

From the above, we are proposing a change in vendor. iBoost is requesting information on the drivers i.e. name, phone number, Thai national ID. They do not require any layer of consent but acts on our behalf as a background check partner. 

[+*T&Cs*+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/158z4bVPEc0x7qd_8wLGiJIG9_BkM_R4kGvrTVSXRoBs/edit#heading=h.waa1qgrp5oc3]+*:*+

We do not want to create multiple frictions for the drivers to perform the checks; therefore, we are proposing a mass update of T&Cs to existing drivers and a new consent flow to the onboarding process of new drivers. The GoogleForm we have previously created results in some drivers not completing the form. We do not want this problem to reoccur. Our goal is to minimize any action required by the drivers to fill any form. The T&Cs will be updated and we will communicate to the drivers via in-app and SMS on the drivers have to pay for the checks.

Due to the urgency and importance of the safety topic in Thailand, I appreciate any support and advise on how we can make this process as seamless for the drivers as possible. Thank you.

{quote}Do you have an RFC document related to this project that relates to using delivery notes for building entrance detection?

We need to conduct the assessment and ensure we cover this in our privacy notices{quote}

Usually product-led initiatives have an RFC, this is an engineering/research driven initiative to improve the accuracy of delivery locations and has no dedicated RFC document.

We want to make sure Couriers are led to the correct building. Their GPS movement data is noisy and sometimes when compared with a map it crosses into several buildings. In order to pinpoint the correct building we compare the address information and user pin location (provided by the user) with map data. This way we can identify which address belongs to which building more accurately.

 There can still be ambiguity on which side the courier entered the building. To improve this, we are looking for contextual clues in the information that the user provided that we can again compare with the map. Examples are: "2nd barrier, building behind the Mega Image", "enter from balcescu street", "opposite lidl supermarket". Interpreting this type of data requires a language model, hence this request

The expectation is that this effort will improve:

* the accuracy by which we select the correct building for an address
* the accuracy by which we identify the entrance of the building to set the delivery location accurately

Q&A:

*Refresher - what are ls (lengthscale) and eta (signal variance)*
	ls - is "how many time points" we need to move the GP to ETA (i.e. horizontal variance - how slow and how fast a metric changes)
	eta - is by how much the GP can change over the ls (i.e. vertical - how much in size a metric changes)

*ETA ls is defined with InverseGamma (in pymc marketing). Why exactly?*

([https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse-gamma_distribution|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse-gamma_distribution|smart-link] )
NOTE: Learned in Max Kochurov’s lectures that Eta and LS is OK to pass with numbers, not necessarily priors

*Why should we use softplus? Will it ensure positivity of effects?*

Presumably, yes

*For prior we can use .prior() and .prior_linearized(). What’s the difference?*

* prior_linearized() gives access to the variable (prior() - does not do it directly)
* Why do we need access to HSGP coefficients at all?
* linearizied prior used in hierarchical setting: [https://gist.github.com/kforeman/692542430469d016f84a17f230d8500b|https://gist.github.com/kforeman/692542430469d016f84a17f230d8500b|smart-link] 

*HSGP is defined with m and (c or L). How to know what's best?*

* {{gp = pm.gp.HSGP(m=[100], c=1.2, cov_func=cov_func)}}
* m is approximation parameter. larger M → sharper fluctuations available, but more computing time. Can be even more than n observations. (increase of m gives more explained data (lower MAPE))
* L and c are related (essentially, there’s only L, c is a lazy way to infer L):
** L means indeces (i.e. days) for which you are applying the inference. 
** c is a lazy way to set L by taking the max integer and multiplying it by c (that is why I want to normalize dates to have the 0 in the middle)
*** Moving the c (from 1.2) to 1 and to 2 did not give improvement (actually worsened the results)
** Pushing 0 to the middle does not actually provide big advantage (does not change results at all). But seems a good thing that everybody does
** *NOTE:* In HSGP you want the data to be a bit beyond your actual data (i.e. the process is assumed to stretch a bit forward and backward)

*What is X in pymc-marketing?*
	X=time_index (time in integer: [0,1,2,3,4]),
	X_mid - is when you put 0 to the middle

*pymc-marketing do this, should we be doing it as well?*

{{centered_f = f - f.mean(axis=0) + 1}}

*What is dims in HSGP coef?*

* this is related to how HSGP approximates the process. More specifically, this is the m in {{gp = pm.gp.HSGP(m=[30], c=1.2, cov_func=cov_func)}}


[*Here*|https://github.com/pymc-labs/pymc-marketing/blob/39d38b781ff37cdef54676f5a9c3124f1b2ab3ef/pymc_marketing/mmm/tvp.py#L165C5-L165C40] *the .T is used to transpose, here* [*not*|https://www.pymc.io/projects/docs/en/stable/api/gp/generated/classmethods/pymc.gp.HSGP.prior_linearized.html]*. How to work around that?*



*How to run hierarchical HSGP?*

Check here: [https://discourse.pymc.io/t/hierarchical-two-layer-gaussian-process/5715|https://discourse.pymc.io/t/hierarchical-two-layer-gaussian-process/5715|smart-link] 

And prepared gist alse here: [https://gist.github.com/bwengals/90e79d64fe9e2d496a048f0b2c6d33da|https://gist.github.com/bwengals/90e79d64fe9e2d496a048f0b2c6d33da|smart-link] 

[https://www.pymc.io/projects/examples/en/latest/gaussian_processes/HSGP-Advanced.html|https://www.pymc.io/projects/examples/en/latest/gaussian_processes/HSGP-Advanced.html|smart-link] 

*Should we prefer .Latent() to .HSGP()*

* Latent seems to give the same result as HSGP with high m

*How to push the process to decrease MAPE and 'overfit'?*

* setting sigma=1 when modelling the noise - can give impact (but so far only for linear cases

*Using different backends - is there any difference?*
GPs are sometimes taking long to sample through - checked some other sampling backends: 	

* {{numpyro}} and {{blackjax}} give similar improvement (x2+) 	
* {{nutpie}} does not give that improvement



Also useful links on how smoothing with prior works:

[https://www.pymc.io/projects/examples/en/latest/gaussian_processes/GP-smoothing.html|https://www.pymc.io/projects/examples/en/latest/gaussian_processes/GP-smoothing.html|smart-link]

Hi [~accountid:5f323214e11542004633f8af] - apologies for the delay on this. I have synced with the team and our thoughts are as follows:

* As mentioned below, although I appreciate there is a clear _business case_ for simplifying the process and not asking for driver consent, this does not change the _legal_ position (i.e., the requirements of the GDPR) - to change a driver’s personal data, we need the request to either come from the driver or from someone *properly authorised*. As such, the current process should still be kept as it is - otherwise, we will be non-compliant with the GDPR and risk possible data breaches.
* As discussed over Slack, to streamline the process, an option could be to produce a *standard form document* that we can provide to Fleet Owners to be passed on to the driver (and which the driver would then sign), which would constitute the driver’s authorisation for the FO to change the driver’s data on the driver’s behalf. However, before we prepare such a document, {color:#ff5630}*it is worth considering the operational impact*{color} here. In particular, can you confirm the following:
** How do we envision that the driver would sign this document? Would it be wet-ink or e-signature? A concern here is that it may be overly burdensome for the driver to print out the document, sign it, scan it and send it to the fleet.
** If a fleet decided to sign the document on the driver’s behalf to save time and without sending t to the driver, how would we check for fraud?

Dear Wahidullah,

Thank you for your data subject rights request, which was received by us on 22 July 2024.

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person.

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, the law requires a data controller such as ourselves to protect the rights of third parties (for example, passengers). Furthermore, we must point out that we are not required to disclose documents or otherwise provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

We share copies of the personal data we hold about you to which you are entitled. This includes:

* Date on which you started providing transportation services via the Bolt platform as an independent contractor: 10 October 2019; and
* Order history between 10 October 2019 and 14 June 2021.

Regarding your request for invoices between 10 October 2019 and 14 June 2021, we require additional time to fulfil this request as we have deemed it to be complex. Under relevant data protection legislation, we are permitted to extend the deadline for response by up to an additional two months, which we have determined to be necessary in this instance. We would like to provide you with the following reasons for this extension:

* We have experienced technical difficulties in retrieving the information.

We are committed to providing you with a response to your request as soon as possible. We anticipate that we will be able to respond to your request no later than 22 October 2024. If we are able to provide you with the invoices sooner, we will of course do so.

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

*Your rights* 

You have the right to request rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing of personal data concerning you or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You have the right to complain directly to the appropriate supervisory authority and seek a judicial remedy. 

If you have any additional questions, please let us know.

Yours sincerely,

*Bolt*

Hey [~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a]. Most of the cases are not privacy questions purely, we are providing advice because everything we do re rider ratings can become a privacy issue and be spotted by regulators. In other words, while it’s not a DSR, it’s very important to us how the end-result looks like.  

* *(A) “I want to know more about my Rider Rating” -* agree, not a privacy request if the user wants to kn
* *(B) “I want to know why my Rider Rating has dropped”* 
* *(C) “I want to increase my Rider Rating”*
** For B and C - we need to ask the requestor what kind of questions we are expecting. From the way it’s phrased, I don’t think the rider wants to increase the rating - they want to know why it dropped. In this case, we can refer to the Blog and perhaps the Marketplace Conduct guidelines ([https://bolt.eu/en/legal/marketplace-guidelines-terms/|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/marketplace-guidelines-terms/|smart-link] ) and say that the ratings drop when the drivers rate them. The rider can be advised to follow the guidelines
** For B and C - if the requestor gives us examples of specific questions, then we can know how deep should we go. 
* *(D) “I want to know my Rider Rating for a specific trip”* - agree, no comments
* *(E) “I want you to provide me with all individual Rider Ratings that I have ever received”* - let’s discuss during team meeting. I suggest asking the stats on how many cases like this we receive on average per month/year. If it’s up to 10 - perhaps it makes sense to escalate it to the privacy team to take care of.

Hey!

This is an interesting approach by the Philippines. I think we could sign this document, but there are some instances here:

→ Repatriation: yes, this is something that can be enforced as this can be considered an additional benefit.

→ Termination clauses: on the whole, more-or-less the same as the legal grounds in EE. Tho, this agreement extends them a bit - this means they might not be enforceable (_we cannot terminate the employee if they don’t celebrate Christmas - even if this is the custom here_).

→ If the employee is working in EE, I don’t think we can alter the applicable jurisdiction/settlement procedure. They have the right to apply for the court hearing(s) and so do we. Any conditions that are worse than the minimum set by the law, are considered null. We can agree to the arbitration terms, but they are not enforceable, in my opinion.

→ Amendments to the agreement: this can be stated in the annex that some prior consent has to be acquired from PH officials, but the employment contract can be changed/amended by the consent of the parties.

Hi [~accountid:5f323214e11542004633f8af] 

According to the Estonian AML law, we need to notify FIU about this transaction. We have done this already and now we need to wait for them to come back to us before we can determine what are the next steps. 

I also replied to the slack conversation about this. Will paste it here to avoid having the same conversation in multiple channels:


”I understand your concern, but consider the risk here might be higher/different than the fleet owner going to press. The risk is related to compliance and sanctions compliance with our banking partners we use for payouts, which could compromise all our operations and its is way broader than this specific case. We have had discussions around the Sanctions issue in general between Legal, Fin. Reg. and Partner Payments and we still need to define an internal process for these Sanctions hits/suspicions we are not able to rule out. 

In Estonia (consider the payer is Bolt Operations OU) the AML law require to report any sanctions suspicion ruled or not fully ruled out. We have done this already and we need to wait for the Estonian FIU to come back to us (they have up to 60 days to do it). After this, we will have more clarity on what are the next steps to take. 

In regard to this specific case of the F.O in Germany, what happened is that one of our banking partners was not able to complete this payment without providing a specific reason other than might be sanctions related and it could be directly and indirectly connected to the recipient. We made our own sanctions checks on this F.O. and could not find anything (as it could also be indirectly linked to a person or transaction, hard to know from our end what is the reason and be able to rule out any suspicions).

In terms of what can be communicated to the F.O., we must inform him our banking parter rejected the transaction (multiple times, as I see from the comments in the Jira ticket but [@jaak.kaljula|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U02LE7C65PA] can confirm) without giving further explanation. Therefore, and as they are already informed, we cannot do business with them and they were offboarded. Even if the F.O. goes to a debt collection agency, I still need to wait for the Estonian FIU to come back to us.”

V/Ref.ª DS.REC-110/2024/183 FW: Bolt - Hugo Miguel Broa - Ocasião Divertida, Lda 

Exmos.(a) Senhor(as),

Recebemos a vossa notificação para prestação de informações relativamente à Reclamação supra identificada.

De acordo com a legislação em vigor, a ” prestação do serviço de TVDE pode ser remunerada pela aplicação de uma ou mais tarifas à distância percorrida e/ou ao tempo despendido no transporte, ou pela aplicação de um preço fixo determinado antes da contratação do serviço.” 

Neste sentido, os termos e condições da Bolt aceites pelo operador TVDE ao serviço do qual o motorista presta serviços estabelecem:

“5.2. Para a prestação dos Serviços de Transporte, o Operador TVDE e a Bolt acordam que o Preço da Viagem será calculado tendo por base fatores variáveis, incluindo (mas não limitado a) a distância da viagem conforme determinado pelo sistema GPS, a duração da viagem, a flutuação do mercado local, bem como quaisquer taxas aplicáveis. As partes reconhecem que é possível que o Preço da Viagem seja inferior ou superior à estimativa inicialmente apresentada ao Utilizador na App Bolt.

5.3. Em alternativa ao Preço da Viagem calculado de acordo com a cláusula 5.2, a App Bolt poderá também propor um preço fixo pré-determinado que, em caso de aceitação pelo Utilizador, corresponde ao Preço da Viagem a cobrar no final do Serviço de Transporte independentemente da distância da viagem ou da sua duração. A proposta de preço fixo pré-determinado é comunicada ao Utilizador e ao Operador TVDE (eventualmente, através do Motorista que atue em sua representação) através da App Bolt antes da prestação do Serviço de Transporte. “

No caso em análise, a Bolt comunicou antes da aceitação da viagem ao passageiro o preço no montante de *39.78€ (onde este poderia também ver um desconto no preço, assumido pela Bolt)* e ,em conformidade, o preço de *39.78€* ao motorista TVDE em representação do seu operador TVDE. A proposta de preço foi aceite por ambas as partes. 

Uma revisão de preço foi solicitada pelo motorista após a conclusão da viagem, sendo que a equipa interna da Bolt concluiu que o preço encontra-se em conformidade com os nossos termos e condições, nomeadamente:

* não foi alterado o destino durante a viagem;
* a viagem não foi mais longa do que o inicialmente estimado e
* não existem outras circunstâncias inesperadas que tivessem alterado as características da viagem.

Estando o preço em conformidade com a regulamentação em vigor e os termos e condições da Bolt, a Bolt entende não existirem fundamentos para uma revisão de preço.

Esperamos que a informação acima seja suficiente para esclarecer todas as questões mas mantemo-nos disponíveis para qualquer esclarecimento adicional. Em anexo segue a cópia da informação remetida ao Reclamante.

Melhores cumprimentos,

*Can you please review this case and advise the team what to do:*



*Issue:* the driver made a request to delete his account. It's a fleet driver so local ops contacted the fleet in order to have an approval for driver's account deletion. Fleet did not approve the account deletion and the driver was advised accordingly. 

*Explanation:* we do not have any official process/guideline at Bolt related to getting the fleet’s approval for account deletion. However, as the team elaborated 

* “_In our competitive fleet market, Fleet Owners have significant influence over the account deletion process, as fleet drivers are employees of the fleet and are provided with vehicles by the fleet. The Fleet Owner is ultimately responsible for deciding whether a driver should be released, as they were the original employer. Ideally, we’d prefer to receive deletion requests directly from Fleet Owners. However, if a driver tries to bypass paying debts by contacting us directly, we’ll need to reach out to the fleet._
* _When a fleet driver requests to delete their account, we need to check with the fleet to make sure they agree to the release. This ensures that any debts, fines, or damage issues are handled properly. Deleting fleet driver accounts without fleet approval could affect our relationships with fleets in a competitive market. Additionally, drivers with debts might create new accounts to keep working, which could lead to more issues for the fleets._
* _If a driver’s request for account deletion is denied, they are instructed to contact their fleet directly. This accelerates the resolution process and allows the driver to transition to another fleet or become a private driver more efficiently.”_

*Request:* Given the above, please specify what should we do in such cases and what arguments can be sent to drivers in relation to their personal data.

My stand is that we should delete the driver’s account and personal data as Bolt is considered a data controller for such data. However, we can rely on the exemption that such data/account are still necessary for Bolt - purpose still exists.


*To note:* This particular driver threats to go to the court for Bolt refusing to delete his personal data.

Important changes in 7.2:

* Redis 7.2 uses a new format (version 11) for RDB files, which is incompatible
with older versions.
* Add a few low level event loop metrics to help diagnose latency ([+#11963+|https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/11963])
* Cluster SHARD IDs are no longer visible in the cluster nodes output,
introduced in 7.2-RC1. ([+#10536+|https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/10536], [+#12166+|https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/12166])
* Add cluster-announce-human-nodename - a unique identifier for a node that is
be used in logs for debugging ([+#9564+|https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/9564])

Performance:

* Significant memory optimization of small list type keys ([+#11303+|https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/11303])
* Significant memory optimization for small set type keys ([+#11290+|https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/11290])
* Significant memory optimization for large sets ([+#11595+|https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/11595])
* Significant speed optimization in ZRANGE replies WITHSCORES in case of integer scores ([+#11779+|https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/11779])
* Significant speed optimization in double replies, mainly sorted sets commands ([+#10587+|https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/10587])
* Optimize the performance of commands with multiple keys in cluster mode ([+#11044+|https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/11044])
* Incrementally reclaim OS page cache of RDB file ([+#11248+|https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/11248])
* Improve memory management of cluster bus links when there is a large number of pending messages ([+#11343+|https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/11343])
* Minor performance improvement for workloads that use commands without pipelining ([+#11220+|https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/11220])

Hi [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] - I include my thoughts on this one below. As mentioned, it is a bank holiday on Monday in the UK and so I will not be around for the deadline, so I will reassign the ticket back to you for now, but if this is extended then we can discuss again next week 🙂 

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
{color:#6554c0}*In summary:*{color}

* *Key practical question:* On the Bolt side, can we delete individual data points on a driver’s account, or can we only delete the entire account? I assume the answer is the latter - but if it was the former, then we could consider deleting certain data points in response to these types of request, and leaving others.
* Bolt definitely needs to acknowledge these requests in some way, either by actioning them or providing valid reasoning for why we are refusing to action them.
* We _may_ have grounds for refusing to delete on the grounds of continuing necessity, particularly with regards to exercising legal claims.
* I would definitely check with the wider team for their views, and my analysis here is based on a very quick skim of the facts in the time available, as well as a very high-level understanding of the role of fleets / processes at Bolt. 


{panel}

----

{color:#4c9aff}*Issue 1 - Does Bolt need to concern itself with these kinds of requests?*{color}

Yes. As you say, Bolt is the data controller of the driver’s data. As such, when Bolt receives this kind of request, we need to either: (a) action it; or (b) write to the user clearly explaining why we cannot action it (as well as flagging to the user that they have the right to complain to a regulatory authority  seek a judicial remedy), given that this is a valid personal data erasure request.

----

{color:#4c9aff}*Issue 2 - Can Bolt delete certain kinds of data, and leave others?*{color}

An important practical question here is whether we can delete any data on the driver’s account on a granular level. 

If we can, and we receive a request from a driver to delete their data, we should consider whether there is any data that we can delete from the driver’s account that is _not_ needed for the fleet to settle debts / fines / damage issues. If so, and there are no other legal / compliance / practical reasons for retaining it, then the most compliant approach that Bolt could take would be to delete this ‘extra’ data, and only retain the data that is necessary for the fleet to settle debts / fines / damage issues.

However, I am assuming that we only have operational capacity to delete an entire account - {color:#ff5630}*is this correct*{color}? If so, then it sounds like there is a sensible reason to not delete the account until the FO has given the green light (as doing so could allow drivers to circumvent their financial obligations to their employer), and so we need to think about how to frame refusing the erasure request wholesale… (see below).

----

{color:#4c9aff}*Issue 3 - On what grounds can we refuse to action these requests?*{color}

IMO, Bolt could have grounds for pushing back on these types of deletion requests. Our specific reasoning for refusing to action the request will depend on the data at-issue / the relevant legal basis. However, if the driver is asking to delete their _whole_ account, then I suppose we can take a holistic approach and include all of the below to some degree in a response to the driver:

* We can argue that processing the data is still necessary for the purpose for which it was collected (although it may be difficult to argue that retaining the _whole account_ is still necessary);
* If we rely on consent, then the driver has a right to withdraw their consent and request deletion. However, we could argue that retaining the data is necessary for the establishment, exercise and defence of legal claims (as the FO may need it as part of settling outstanding debts / claims with the driver); and
* If we rely on legitimate interest, we argue that there is an overriding interest to continue processing the data (i.e., the FO needs to settle debts / fines / damage issues with the user).

Including all of the above in a single response may be the best approach. For example, we could use something like this:

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
_Dear [Name],_

_We write in response to your erasure request, which we received on [date]._

_We have reached out to your employer, [Fleet owner], who has confirmed that maintaining your account on the Bolt platform continues to be necessary to ensure that any debts / fines / damages issues are settled with your employer before your account can be closed. Applicable data protection law therefore permits us to deny your erasure request because, in particular, continued processing of your personal data is currently necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims._

_If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy._

_If you have any additional questions, please let us know._

_Yours sincerely,_

_Bolt_
{panel}

However, my thoughts above are based on a very high-level understanding of the role of fleet owners here and of some of Bolt’s processes / positions. As such, I would strongly recommend checking this with the rest of the team for their views, as we need to be careful how we position this.

{quote}* Can you advise on whether this integration would be a real-time integration, eg user leaves a note in the app → ChatGPT API processes this → Provides the structured result to the Courier app?
** If no, is this for our backend analysis only, eg we analyse it with the help of chatgpt to get structured data and proceed with building entrance detection in the courier app?{quote}

The first step of this initiative is backend analysis only (i.e., offline analysis): we will analyze historical user notes with ChatGPT, get structured data back, then use that structured data to improve our building entrance detection algorithm. 

The building entrances we detect are stored in our backend and whenever a courier delivers to a certain location, we look up the building entrance at that location, and show the entrance as a point on the map in the courier app. Structured output from ChatGP is not used directly nor shown to couriers in real-time in any way.

However, depending on our research, we may decide to develop real-time processing of user notes with ChatGPT.

As an example, we sometimes detect multiple entrances for a building. In such a case, a user note like “enter from balcescu street” provides relevant context to selecting the appropriate entrance (i.e., the entrance on Balcescu street). As such, when a delivery request is made to our systems, we may decide to process the user note with ChatGPT, in real-time, to extract structured data from the note and use that data to select the entrance shown in the courier app (but structured data extracted from the note is not shown to our courier directly).

Overall, there are three potential scenarios for our ChatGPT usage:

# Offline processing of historical user notes which is used to improve building entrance detection. Structured data from historical user notes is not shown directly to couriers.
# Online/real-time processing of the user note associated with an order to help select the relevant building or building entrance. Structured data extracted by ChatGPT from this user note is not shown directly to couriers.
# Online/real-time processing of the user note associated with an order. Structured data from the user note is shown directly in the courier app to help improve courier navigation. However, we do not yet have a clear plan for this scenario (i.e., what data can be extracted, how to extract it, what navigation hints to show to our couriers and how), but it may be worth updating our privacy policy to include this scenario as well as it may enable future work.

*Handling Dashcam Recordings in Compliance with GDPR*

# *Preliminary Assessments and Privacy Notices*:

* Conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) and Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) before using dashboard cameras in Bolt Drive vehicles in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and the Czech Republic. 
* Update Bolt Drive's Privacy Notices to inform users about data processing.

# *Technical and Organisational Measures*:

* Implement measures to ensure data minimisation, such as adjusting cameras to capture only necessary footage (e.g., road collisions) and disabling unnecessary functions (e.g., zoom, audio recording).
* Ensure that drivers cannot alter camera settings and that cameras are active only when the vehicle is in use.

# *Informing Data Subjects*:

* Display clear signs on vehicles with dashboard cameras, including a camera pictogram, the data controller's contact information, the purpose of data processing, and a link to Bolt's detailed privacy notice.
* Signs should be visible and in both English and the local language.

# *Data Retention and Deletion*:

* Retain footage for a maximum of 72 hours, unless justified otherwise.
* Delete footage automatically if no incidents occur. Retain only relevant footage for ongoing investigations or claims, and delete it once the case is resolved.

# *Data Processing Agreement*:

* Establish a Data Processing Agreement with any service provider involved in handling the dashcam recordings.

*Next steps:*

* Next week, we will share with you our assessment of the privacy risk associated with a Chinese service provider. 
* We will begin working on DPIAs, LIAs and changes to Privacy Notices.
* Once the assessments are approved by the DPO, we will begin working with the hardware team on the dashcam stickers.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
{color:#403294}*Summary*{color}:

* _General_ requests about how rider ratings work / why a user’s rating has gone down are not necessarily requests to be dealt with by the privacy team. Bolt can respond to such requests by referring the user to public information materials. I have included some suggested draft wording below.
* Requests that ask for _specific_ rider ratings, _data processing_ in relation to rider ratings, and/or questions about _privacy law_ in relation to rider ratings, should be reviewed by the privacy team. The three examples you have highlighted in the table do not obviously fall within these three scenarios - Can you please provide us examples of more specific requests that we have been receiving from users regarding rider ratings, so that we can advise on whether these are the kinds of requests that fall under Privacy’s remit?
* Can you also please provide us with a summary of how many requests we receive from riders per month / year asking for specific rider ratings (or for a copy of every single rider rating they have ever received)? 
{panel}

----

*(A) “I want to know more about my Rider Rating”*

{color:#4c9aff}*Thoughts:*{color}

* This *does not obviously fall within the remit of a privacy issue* / request, as it is technically not their personal data.
* As such, where a request is ambiguously phrased (i.e., it can be interpreted as a general request for an _explanation_ of / _more information_ on rider ratings), we should lean on the ambiguity to avoid getting into the weeds of whether or not we can provide individual rider ratings. Instead, the rider should be referred to *general informative materials* on rider ratings. It should then be left to the rider to request more specific information, if they want it.
* We should also *avoid* characterising general requests for information about rider ratings as ‘data subject rights requests’, as technically these do not yet qualify. As such, CS knowledge materials should include an instruction to +not+ send the DSAR acknowledgement template unless the rider is specifically requesting their personal data / information about data processing or the questions is relevant to privacy law.
* The below is an example of a response which could be included in the CS KB. CS could then deal with these types of requests.

{color:#36b37e}*Draft Response:*{color}

_Dear [Rider],_

_Thank you for your request for more information about your Rider Rating._

_Please note that your Rider Rating as it appears in your Bolt app is calculated as an average rating based on your ratings from the previous 365 days. Each rating is from 1 to 5, as provided by the driver at the end of each trip. Further information on Rider Ratings can be found here:_ [_https://bolt.eu/en/rider-rating/_|https://bolt.eu/en/rider-rating/]_._

_If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve your concerns. If you have any additional questions, please let us know._

_Yours sincerely,_

*_Bolt_*

----

*(B) “I want to know why my Rider Rating has dropped”*

{color:#4c9aff}*Thoughts:*{color}

* As above, we should be careful not to characterise these as privacy issues / requests unless there is an obvious reason to do so. For example, if the rider requests “_I want to know how my personal data is processed to calculate my rider rating_”, then this would be a data subject rights request - on the other hand, the above wording is more ambiguous, and is not obviously relevant to privacy. As such, please could you provide us with some {color:#ff5630}*more specific examples of how these types of requests are worded*{color}?
* If the requests do not explicitly refer to individual ratings or personal data processing / data protection law issues, then we can send a similar response to *(A)* above and perhaps also Marketplace Conduct guidelines ([https://bolt.eu/en/legal/marketplace-guidelines-terms/|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/marketplace-guidelines-terms/|smart-link] ) and say that the ratings drop when the drivers rate them. The rider can be advised to follow the guidelines.
* This guidance could be included in the CS KB. CS could then deal with these types of requests.

----

*(C) “I want to increase my Rider Rating”*

{color:#4c9aff}*Thoughts:*{color}

* As above, we should be careful not to characterise these as privacy issues / requests unless there is an obvious reason to do so. As such, please could you provide us with some {color:#ff5630}*more specific examples of how these types of requests are worded*{color}?
* If the requests do not explicitly refer to individual ratings or personal data processing / data protection law issues, then we can send a similar response to *(A)* above and perhaps also Marketplace Conduct guidelines ([https://bolt.eu/en/legal/marketplace-guidelines-terms/|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/marketplace-guidelines-terms/|smart-link] ) and say that the ratings drop when the drivers rate them. The rider can be advised to follow the guidelines.
* This guidance could be included in the CS KB. CS could then deal with these types of requests.

----

*Requests pertaining to individual ratings*

If the rider is asking for specific rider ratings (e.g., “I want my rating for this trip” or “I want all ratings I have ever received”), this could be construed as a data subject request and fall under Privacy’s remit.

As such, can you please provide us with {color:#ff5630}*a summary of how many such requests we receive from riders per month / year*{color}? This will give us a good idea of how to strategise.

Hi [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] - just wanted to re-flag my questions here before I finalise this and respond - IMO, this seems to be a simple case of explaining to the user at a very high level how rider ratings are calculated, and then leaving it at that - however, I note from your instructions that we need to provide the user with a list of their rides - *Why? Let me know if I am missing something here.*

If I am not, then I propose responding to Judith with the below.

----

Hi Judith - Apologies for the delay on this.

The reason for the mismatch between rider ratings on the App and in Admin is as follows:

* *App*: Average rating is determined by adding together all of the ratings from the last 365 days and dividing the total by 365 (i.e., it is the average for the last year only - see [this article|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PRODWIKI/pages/4615013174/Driver+Rating+Rider#Rider-App]).
* *Admin*: Average rating is determined based on the average of all previous ratings ever received (i.e., not just limited to the past 365 days).

As a result, the user’s average rating from the past 365 days (shown in the App) is lower than the user’s average rating over the course of their entire time with Bolt (shown in Admin). We only share the former with the user.

In terms of responding to the user, I would reply with the following. Please then monitor the ticket for 7 days and close it if we do not receive any follow-ups.

_Dear Daniel,_

_Thank you for your request for more information about your Rider Rating._

_Please note that your Rider Rating as it appears in your Bolt app is calculated as an average rating based on your ratings from the previous 365 days. Each rating is from 1 to 5, as provided by the driver at the end of each trip. Further information on Rider Ratings can be found here:_ [_https://bolt.eu/en/rider-rating/_|https://bolt.eu/en/rider-rating/]_._

_If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve your concerns. If you have any additional questions, please let us know._

_Yours sincerely,_

*_Bolt_*
